docs.text: 1 National Tsing Hua University Institute of Technology Management Organizational Behavior Fall 2025 Class meets: Wednesday 9am to 11:50am in Room 120, TSMC Building Instructor: Dr. Yu-Wen Liu Language: Chinese Office: Room 851 TSMC Building Office hours: By appointment Contact: ywliu@mx.nthu.edu.tw COURSE OBJECTIVE: After completing the class, you should become familiar with the major concepts of organizational behavior and issues that managers encounter, and with principles, practices and models that help managers deal with these issues. In addition, you should be able to see how the relationships among people within an organization and relationships among organizations influence organizational effectiveness. DETAILS: Each class will include discussion of readings, recent news and cases. Your grade will be based on your performance in the following three categories. I. Classroom Participation (25%) In-class Discussion The learning experience in a course like this one depends heavily on each student being prepared to actively participate in every class session. Positive participation includes attendance, active involvement in all in-class exercises and discussions, and maintenance of a classroom demeanor that encourages the participation of others. You will be evaluated on the quantity as well as the quality of your contribution and insights. Quality comments possess one or more of the following attributes: (a) Contribute to moving the discussion forward; (b) Offer a different, unique and relevant perspective on the issue; (c) Build on other comments of others; and (d) Include some evidence or analysis of inherent tradeoffs, i.e., demonstrate reflective thinking. Individual weekly personal learning note In addition, closing to the end of every class, each student is required to summarize what you have learned in our class on that day in one page. The one-page summary should include both key ideas from each article and your main takeaway from our class discussion. II. Group Assignments (50%) Weekly group presentation for the selected article/book chapter (15% x 2 = 30%) Every week, two groups of students will be responsible for presenting the key ideas from one selected article or textbook chapter and raising some questions for discussion 2 for that week. The presentation should be done within 20 minutes. Additionally, each group needs to provide at least one additional reading on the selected topic which is published after 2015. These readings can be newspaper, magazine, or journal articles. These additional readings can be written in Chinese or English. Choose one reading from the provided additional readings and develop a 10-minute presentation or activity for the chosen reading. We will leave 20 minutes for discussing questions. Final group project (20%) Each group needs to select one company/business field/industry, identify the challenges the company/business field/industry currently faces through analyzing secondary data, interviewing or observing onsite, and come up with potential solutions to fix the problems that the company/business field/industry are facing. On Oct 29, 2025, each group will hand in their target company/business field/industry and their problems for the term project. All groups need to hand in and present your progress report of the final project on Nov. 26, 2025. The final presentation will be held on Dec 10 & 17, 2025. The content of presentation includes the components below: One company/business field/industry, the challenges, potential solutions, business ideas, and your intended goal. The more details, the better. Final group project delivery Before your group presentation, the ppt file should be sent to the following address ywliu@mx.nthu.edu.tw before 5 pm on Sunday. Please Note that, the final grade on group related assignments might not be the same for all members on a team if someone does not contribute equally to the team projects. Please note that the credit for each team member in the same team might be different if most of your teammates are not satisfied with your contribution. Team Member Assessments: Every team member will • Develop a substantive assessment (min 30 words each) on each team member’s contributions. • Assign a % in 5% increments (e.g. 80%, 95%, 100%, 110%, etc) to each of the other team members, insuring that the total of your percentages adds up to the number of other team members x 100% (so 3 other team members = 300%, 4 other team members = 400%, etc) • Post his/her Team Member Assessments to Assignment. III. Taiwanese Enterprises in Global Markets: A Learning Journey (25%) This project : “世界”，我來了: 跟著台商的腳步走 is to explore the challenges of global expansion from a Taiwanese perspective by learning from Taiwanese enterprises abroad and expatriates. Further instructions will be provided in class. OTHER POLICIES OR NOTES: • Do not miss classes. However, you are allowed to be absent from the class for two times, no questions asked. You might want to use the freebee wisely. Beyond that, your grade will be significantly affected. • Be on time for classes 3 • Turn off cellular phones • Do not accept late assignments • Do not cheat on exams • Attendance ≠participation Any violation of the above rules will seriously adversely affect your grade The conduct used in managing student use of the AI: Conditionally open; please specify how generative AI is used in course output. 4 TENTATIVE WEEKLY SESSION TOPICS Session 1: Rewards - Duncan, W. A.課程內容／Course Content

透過本課程，學生可以對博士論文的研究課題，能有正確且有效地構建文獻探討的能力。
This course introduces the micro-level and macro-level of technology management
with respect to related theories, research fields and academic journals. The
micro-level comprises open innovation, entrepreneurial management, resource-
bassed view, social innovation, social business models, etc.

The macro-level consists of the extent and theories of technology policy,
including national,industrial and regional innovation system, triple-helix model
of innovation, innovation ecosystem, university-industry relation policy,
entrepreneurial universities and social entrepreneurship and ecosystem etc.

Through this course, students will be able to undertake appropriate literature
review with respect to their doctoral dissertation.
Evaluation
1. Participation & Attendance: 20%
2. Presentation & Discussion: 40%
3. Final report: 40%

Weekly Presentation
1. 2 or 3 papers/week
2. Each paper:
1 presenter+1 discussant
Presentation: 20 minutes
Discussant: 10 minutes
Q&A: 20 minutes

Guideline for research
proposal: A critical review
1. Contents
(1) title
(2) Research questions
(3) Research gaps
(4) A critical literature review/theoretical background/hypothesis
development

The length of research proposal is at least five pages but at most 10 pages
with references excluded.

Week Topic

1. Introduction: Introduction to the course and the field
of technology management.
2. The scope, organizations, journals and conferences of TM
3. Emerging new issues of TIM: Transformative innovation policy, smart city
4. The evolutionary perspective on TIM
5. National systems of innovation, triple-helix model of innovation, innovation
ecosystems
6. Research commercialization, Academic entrepreneurship & Entrepreneurial
university
7. Research Clinic 1
8. Social Innovation and Its Impact
9. Dynamics and Development of Entrepreneurial Ecosystems
10. Social Innovation Ecosystem and Business Model Innovation
11. Policy Implementation and Critical Analysis of Social Innovation
12.Technological Innovation on Business Models
13.Technology Adoption and Societal Impact
14. Research Clinic 2

docs.text: TSE 5002 Foundation of Quantitative Methods National Tsing Hua University Fall 2025 Instructor: Eric S. Lin Contact Information: Office: CTM 712, Email: slin@mx.nthu.edu.tw, Phone: 574-2729 Time and Location: Monday 9:00-noon, Center of Innovative Incubator 2F-A10 Office Hours: By appointment Course Webpage: Course materials will be available on the web through eeclass. Teaching Assistant: Raktisud You are lucky to have XXX to be your TA. Teaching Assistant Hours: TBA TA will hold the office hours and also be available for consultation on homework. Course Description: TSE 5002 introduces a range of quantitative tools that are commonly used to inform public policy issues. It provides an introduction to descriptive statistics, probability theory, statistical inference, and decision analysis. Our goal is that by the end of this course you will be able to: 1. Take a data set and a broad descriptive policy question (such as “What has happened to income distribution in Taiwan in the last 30 years?”), figure out what statistical analysis would be most appropriate to answer the question, conduct such an analysis, and present the findings in a way that is accessible to policymakers. 2. Identify real world policy situations in which the tools of probability can be used, identify which tools are most relevant, and critically consume policy analysis in which probability is used. 3. Critically consume policy studies/papers/reports in which statistical analysis is used. 4. Use the decision analysis framework as one tool to make personal and professional decisions, and to think about policy problems. Syllabus Fall 2024 The course content is divided into four broad units: (1) Descriptive Statistics, (2) Prob- ability, (3) Statistical Inference, and (4) Regression. Although the aim will remain on the underlying theory, students will be given several opportunities to gain “hand on” experience with real data set through homework assign- ments. I would encourage students to make use of my office hours (or TA’s office hours) during the semester and not wait until the day before the exam. If you are having difficulty with concepts early on, then it is likely that your difficulties will snowball and that there will be insufficient time to deal with your puzzles close to the exams. So please make use of my office hours to sort out difficulties as they arise. Prerequisites: High school algebra/Calculus preferred but not required Suggested Textbook: Basically, I will hand out my own lecture notes which are the summary of textbooks. You may find a similar textbook to the following:  Moore, David S., McCabe, George P., Craig, Bruce A., 2021, Introduction to the prac- tice of statistics (10th Edition), Macmillan Learning. Of course, there are lots of textbooks related to this course. If you have enough time, it would be also beneficial to check out some of the following reference books. References: Note that you don’t need to buy the following books. The book list is just for your reference.  Gujarati, D. N., 2003, Basic Econometrics, McGraw-Hill.  Wooldridge, J. M., 2003, Introductory Econometrics: A modern approach, South- Western. It is a very popular undergraduate level textbook adopted in US. This book gives a huge amount of empirical examples and illustrates econometric concepts intuitively.  Maddala, G. S., 2001, Introduction to Econometrics, 3rd edition, Wiley. This book is well written and in general is deeper than our textbook. You could also find some fancy topics in Maddala’s book such as bootstrap, Jackknife and GMM.  Kennedy, P. A., 1998, A guide to Econometrics, 4th edition, MIT Press. This book tries to verbally explain difficult econometric ideas and avoids heavy math. – 2 – Syllabus Fall 2024  Pindyck, R. S. and L. R. Rubinfeld, 1998, Econometric Models and Economic Forecasts, McGraw-Hill. Ths is my econometric textbook when I was a junior. It is quite easy to read.  Ramanathan R., 2002, Introductory Econometrics with Applications, 5th edition, South- Western. This book provides a number of practical applications. It is also self-contained. In Chapter 14, the author demonstrates the various steps involved in carrying out an empirical research project.  Johnston and DiNardo, 1997, Econometric Methods, 4th edition, McGraw-Hill. If you are sort of familiar with matrix algebra, it is a nice book to build up the foundation of econometrics. It also serves the bridge to compensate the gap between undergraduate and graduate level econometrics. Software: You are welcome to use any econometric packages such as STATA, R, or Python. Grading: Several problem sets will be passed out during the semester. Although there are benefits to be obtained from working in groups I would advise against students free-riding off other students. There will be two midterms and a final. Note that overdue assignment will NOT be accepted unless accompanied by a medical certificate. The same is true for the exams. Your final grade will base on the following table. Note that NO make-up exam will be offered. docs.text: 1 TSE – Taipei School of Economics and Political Science Syllabus – 2024 FALL [Version May 25, 2024 / with dates to be updated] PERSPECTIVES IN INTERNATIONAL POLITICAL ECONOMY : (國際政治經濟) The Age of Disruption Instructor: Yves Tiberghien (Professor, Dept. of Political Science, UBC and Visiting Professor, TSE) Email: yves.tiberghien@ubc.ca Twitter: @Yves_Global Instructor Bio: https://politics.ubc.ca/persons/yves-tiberghien/ Course Schedule: TBC, lecture room A10 TBC Course Description: This course focuses on the foundations of international political economy, both theoretically and substantively. We initially discuss the various theoretical approaches to IPE, as well as key debates in trade, finance, currency, and investment questions. It also applies the theories and frameworks of IPE to the great questions of our time: the role of governance in markets, changing political economy of development, overcoming the resource curse, the transition of global economic order and hegemonic transition, climate political economy and the green technology revolution, digital and AI political economy, global sanction politics, and others. The session brings all frameworks down to the level of concrete empirical policy questions. Context: This course offers the tools and methods to understand the current remaking of the global economic order since 2008. The time for incremental changes within a stable structure is over. 2 The current battle is over the structure itself. Some pillars remain resilient, and are even expanding, owing to innovative entrepreneurship. But most are fragmenting, decaying, or being redrawn through shifting domestic forces and strategic competition. Will the postwar global order survive? And what explains the different trajectories of key regimes of globalization? We face an age of unprecedented global disruptions and systemic risks. Global governance constitutes one of the key challenges in current international relations and policy- making. As demonstrated by the Covid-19 pandemic, climate change, or the global financial crisis of 2008, global forces often overwhelm a political system that is primarily rooted in fragmented national sovereignty. As the global challenges facing the nations of the earth become more pressing, it becomes critical to address the classical political dilemmas of collective action, global commons, and asymmetry of benefits and costs. Are the dominant players in the system able to make progress in this large battle? The age of a stable US-dominated order is over. We have entered a period of great competition for global rules and norms, a battle between connectivity and fragmentation, and a confrontation between old powers and new rising powers. We are also facing a perfect storm that combines globalization-induced dislocations and a democratic crisis in US and Europe; a large-scale Russian war in Ukraine with ripple effects across the world; a climate change crisis challenging our entire economic model; the greatest pandemic since 1919; a powerful AI-centered/digital technological revolution; the greatest shift in the balance of power in over a century (over 20% of economic power shifting hands from advanced Western democracies to emerging countries between 2000 and 2018); the massive and threatening rise of China; and a US President bent on unraveling the economic and security institutions patiently built since 1944. Asia and soon Africa are rising across the board in all sub- regions, recovering a voice that was lost since pre-colonial times, ushering a much more diverse and multipolar world. According to the IMF’s current forecasts, over 60% of world economic growth will take place in Asia between now and 2030. The two dominant powers, the US and China, are locked into an ever-worsening spiral of trade conflict and security competition, a process made worse by misperceptions and emotional reactions and threatening to engulf the world economy. Is the US intent on destroying the rules-based order it nurtured for decades, in order to stop the rise of China? Or is the US just seeking to adjust rules and the division of benefits? Is China intent on uprooting the Western liberal order, or is China just seeking to gain a bigger voice within existing economic and global institutions, while retaining its historically- derived governance? These little computer 33 chips provide the processing power for everything from cars and iPhones, to unmanned drones and missiles. In Beijing's Made in China 2025 industrial strategy, through which China seeks to move up the value chain to become a high-tech superpower, semiconductor self-sufficiency was one of the targets. Beijing is falling far behind on this target. MIC 2025 stated the aim of meeting 70 per cent of China's demand through domestic production by 2025, but, seven years on, it is only meeting 20 per cent of its domestic needs (by one estimate). The world's leading manufacturer of semiconductors is in fact in Taiwan. The Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dominates more than half the global market, and controls 90 per cent of the cutting edge 5 to 10 nanometre sector (in this industry, size matters; the smaller the chip, the better). Even American companies like Intel outsource a substantial amount of production to TSMC. A tech arms race is underway. In order to control the supply of this small but vital component, China and the US are desperately funnelling money into their own national champions, whilst 'kneecapping' each other's efforts, as my guest Nigel Inkster tells me on this episode. We will study consumers’ constrained choice and demand as well as firms and their production. We will also evaluate the properties of markets, consumers’ and producers’ decisions in the markets and the implications for social welfare. Moreover, we will apply key microeconomic concepts to discuss real world public policies. Main reference: Perloff, Jeffrey M. Microeconomics, 8th edition, Global edition, Pearson, 2018. (You can obtain it from Hwa Tai Publishing (華泰文化) in Taiwan.) Other readings: Journal articles (handed out/assigned in class) Instruction: Most of the material will be lectured. Nevertheless, the students are encouraged to volunteer opinions and raise related issues in the classes. Besides, relevant policy issues will be brought into the class for discussion. 2 Topics: Week 1: Supply and demand Week 2: Consumer’s constrained choice Week 3: Applying consumer theory Week 4: Firms and production Week 5: Cost Week 6: Competitive firms and markets Week 7: Midterm exam Week 8: Applying the Competitive Model Week 9: Monopoly Week 10: Pricing and advertising Week 11: Game theory and Oligopoly I Week 12: Game theory and Oligopoly II Week 13: Uncertainty Week 14: Asymmetric Information I Week 15: Asymmetric Information II Week 16: Final exam Grading Policy: The final grade will be determined by four graded homework, class participation, a midterm exam and a final exam. Each of the homework will comprise 10% of the final grade, class participation will comprise 10% while the midterm and the final exams will comprise 25% of the final grade, respectively. docs.text: 1 Civilizations, Empires and World Order Professor Amitav Acharya Introduction The 21st century is witnessing the end of the “great divergence” between the West and the Rest, which began with the rapid ascent of Western Europe from the 17th century AD onwards and the corresponding decline of the once mighty and wealthy civilizations, such as those of China, India, and Islam. As the global power and idea shifts reshape dynamics of world politics civilizational identities are asserting themselves, creating fears of what Samuel Huntington called a “clash of civilizations”. At the same time, the relative decline of the West, the crisis in the US- led liberal hegemonic order and the increasingly global role of rising powers such as China and India in world affairs are creating new possibilities of both conflict and mutual learning and cooperation between the West and the Rest. Against this backdrop, it has become ever more important to revisit the concepts of “civilization” and “world order”, to examine them from a historical and global perspective, to analyze their interaction and inter-relationships through the ages, and to draw lessons for the present and the future. Aside from its intellectual and analytical purpose, this course has a normative inspiration: to promote greater diversity and inclusion in international studies. According to its foundational narrative, the field of International Relations (IR) was “born” in the UK, and “raised” in the US; hence its labelling as an “American social science” (in Stanley Hoffmann’s phrase),. The conventional study of international relations relies heavily on concepts and practices developed in Europe and the US. This course (due to lack of time, it has a primary focus on China, India and Islam, but brings in others) challenges the Western-centric narrative of IR and opens the door to a Global International Relations (Global IR). While conventional IR uses the nation-state as the unit of analysis, the Global IR approach takes civilizations as the basis unit to explore the multiple types of international systems or world orders, including those that predate the Westphalian system and the rise of the West. If one approaches IR (or “world politics” or “international studies”) with the nation-state as its core unit of analysis, one has less than 400 years of history to play with. This is also the period of the rise and dominance of the West. If one studies IR and related fields from the perspective of civilizations, then one has over 4000 years of human history to reflect on and analyze. In this broad sweep of history, many civilizations have risen, fallen, and reemerged. No civilization can claim a monopoly over ideas or approaches to peace, security, diplomacy, development, human rights, environmental protection, or other related subject-matter of IR. By taking a broad historical perspective, this course aims to uncover the forgotten or marginalized agency of non- Western civilizations in the making of the modern world order, and stress the multiple, global origins of international relations and world politics. This “Global IR” approach not only helps us to better understand the contemporary dynamics of world politics, but also promotes inclusiveness in our increasingly complex, diverse and multicultural world. Learning Objectives 2 In completing this course, students should have developed: 1. Broad familiarity with the history of civilizations and world orders, especially the major civilizations such as China, India, Islam and their impact on the world orders of their times; 2. Ability to analyze the key factors behind the rise of the West and the role played by non- Western civilizations in contributing to it and recognize the historical and cultural forces that have shaped the contemporary world order and will shape the future; 3. Understand and appreciate the multiple foundations of theories and concepts of the discipline of International Relations (IR) and question the present state of IR as a Eurocentric or Western-centric field of study; 4. Enhanced critical thinking, including ability to interpret and present international affairs from multiple cultural and philosophical perspectives; 5. Understand and analyze the key forces shaping world politics today, including the role of emerging powers such as China and India, trends in global governance, conflict and cooperation among nations and states; 6. Sensitivity to, and respect for, diversity and inclusion in the study international affairs. Texts: 1. Henry Kissinger, World Order (New York: Penguin, 2014) 2. Amitav Acharya, The End of American World Order, 2nd edn. (Cambridge, Polity, 2018) Assignments: A. Mid-Term Essay (20%): The “Great Divergence”: Causes, Consequences and Legacies (Deadline Oct 5) The Great Divergence refers to the rise of Western Europe vis-à-vis Asia after the 15th century AD. Your essay should answer the following three questions: • Why did the “great divergence” occur? • Would the West have developed its “killer apps” without imperialism and racism? • What were the principal Eastern contributions to the rise of the West? B. Final Essay (40%) On the topic decided by you after approval from the professor. This must fall within the scope of the syllabus. (Deadline, last day of Class) C. Participation (40%) This will take into consideration regular, punctual attendance; active participation in discussions (asking questions to professor and presenters, commenting on their views as well as those of other students participating in discussions). Schedule: Topics and Readings Class 1. The End of World Order? 3 Video to watch before class, “Civilisation State, Multilateralism and Globalisation” https://doc- research.org/2019/10/civilisation-state-globalisation/ Panel at the 17th Rhodes Forum, Rhodes, Greece, 11-12 October 2019. (you can watch as much as you want, but first half hour is essential and Prof Acharya’s part begins 24.00 minute- ends 30.34 minute) Required: • Henry Kissinger, “The Coronavirus Pandemic Will Forever Alter the World Order,” Wall Street Journal, April 3, 2020, https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-coronavirus-pandemic- will-forever-alter-the-world-order-11585953005 • Amitav Acharya, “How the Coronavirus May Reshape the World Order,” The National Interest, April 18, 2020, https://nationalinterest.org/feature/how-coronavirus-may- reshape-world-order-145972 • Andreas Herberg-Rothe, “The End of The Liberal World Order Is Not The End Of The World,” February 29, 2020, https://www.thepeninsula.org.in/2020/02/29/the-end-of-the- liberal-world-order-is-not-the-end-of-the-world-we-just-need-to-fight-for-freedom-and- equality/ Class 2. Concepts, Approaches and Foundations Required Reading: • Henry Kissinger, World Order, Ch.1: “The Question of World Order” (entire chapter) • Amitav Acharya, The End of American World Order, Ch.1 (“A Multiplex World”-entire chapter) Class 3. The Chinese World Order Required: • John K. Fairbank, ed., The Chinese World Order: Traditional China’s Foreign Relations (Harvard University Press, 1968), Chapter 1: “A Preliminary Framework” • Kissinger, World Order, Ch.6, “Towards an Asian Order” (entire chapter) • Suisheng Zhao, “Reconstruction of Chinese History for a Peaceful Rise,” YaleGlobal, June 13, 2017. http://yaleglobal.yale.edu/content/reconstruction-chinese-history-peaceful- rise • Tingyang Zhao, “Redefining the Concept of Politics via “tianxia”: The Problems, Conditions and Methodology,” World Economics and Politics (Beijing), No.6 (2015): 4- 22. • William Callahan, “Chinese Visions of World Order: Post-hegemonic or a New Hegemony?,” International Studies Review, Vol. 10 (2008), 749–761. http://williamacallahan.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/10/Callahan-TX-ISR-08.pdf • Zhang Feng, “The Tianxia System: World Order in a Chinese Utopia,” http://www.chinaheritagequarterly.org/tien- hsia.php?searchterm=021_utopia.inc&issue=021 Further Reading: 4 • “How Does China’s Imperial Past Shape Its Foreign Policy Today?”, A ChinaFile Conversation, March 15, 2017. http://www.chinafile.com/conversation/how-does-chinas- imperial-past-shape-its-foreign-policy-today • Suisheng Zhao, “Rethinking the Chinese World Order: the imperial cycle and the rise of China,” Journal of Contemporary China, Vol 24, No.96 (2015): 961-982. docs.text: Keywords: China, BRI, Global South, infrastructure, SEZs, extractive industries, environmental impact Course Title: China and the Global South TSE Fall Semester 2025-26 Draft 5-25 [some readings might be swapped out, as this is a field that is changing all the time] Julia C. Strauss Class time: Friday, 10-1 Lecture Room: Office: Office Hours： Fridays 1-2 pm and by appointment online E-mail: js11@soas.ac.uk Description As China is an increasingly important player in world politics, its profile as a non-traditional donor to other developing countries has risen. Yet there is a great deal of (mis)information and at best only partial understanding of its “rise” for the Global South. This weekly seminar seeks to overcome a range of (mis)perceptions about China and the Global South that are regularly (re)told and (re)presented in the open media and in think tanks outside China. After considering what is and is not different about China’s approaches to development and aid, we disaggregate “China” as comprising a multiplicity of actors who “go out” to the Global South in search of investment, aid, and employment in quite different sectors. Weeks 5-7 concentrate on what China makes available to the Global South in terms of infrastructure and investment; Weeks 8-9 turn to the sheer scale and local impacts what China’s rapid industrial growth has meant for primary commodities from the Global South. Weeks 10-11 address questions of China’s “soft power” and environmental impacts in the Global South. Throughout the class we will focus on the ways in which neither China nor countries in the Global South are unified: each is comprised of an ever shifting range of different political, social, and economic actors. After Week 12, we will shift to discussion and presentation of students’ final projects. Course Objectives For students to: 1) Develop greater understanding of the drivers behind China’s sets of relationships with the Global South 2) Develop critical awareness of the rhetoric and claims for and against China’s growing relationships with the Global South through the BRI 3) Hone critical ability to analyse particular instances of China’s projects in the Global South 4) Develop critical and writing skills in policy analysis through the writing of short policy briefs and a longer piece of policy analysis Course Delivery Until the last week in November, will be face to face, and we will meet weekly. Once we shift to “Flipped learning” in the last two weeks of the semester before the examination period, there will be no regularly scheduled class, but I will continue to be available for consultation remotely. Until Week Eleven, the normal format of the seminar will be that I will lecture for a bit more than an hour, followed by a short break, and the rest of the time will be given over to student presentation, discussion, and other exercises TBA. Weeks Eleven and Twelve will be devoted to student presentation of their final projects and discussion. Weeks Thirteen and Fourteen are “Flipped Learning” from then until the Monday of Exam Week, you should be working on your policy report/ final project. There will be no final exam. Course Requirements A) Reading Requirements All students will be expected to have done the reading for the weekly seminar an advance of the class meeting itself. I try to mix up longer, often more academic articles or book chapters with shorter policy or opinion pieces. But if you are to get much at all out of this class, then you need to come to class prepared, and this means having engaged with the reading and the topic before the seminar! B) While there are no specific textbooks for this class, and the topic is changing so rapidly that I will almost certainly have to swap out individual readings as new ones become available, there are several book length treatments of the topic that are especially noteworthy that I hope that the library will procure: 1. Min Ye, The Belt Road and Beyond: State-Mobilized Globalization in China: 1998–2018 (Cambridge University Press, 2020) 2. David Lampton, Selina Ho, and Cheng-chwee Kuik, Rivers of Iron: Railroads and Chinese Power in Southeast Asia (University of California Press 2022) 3. Miriam Driessen, Tales of Hope, Tastes of Bitterness: Chinese Road Builders in Ethiopia (Hong Kong University Press, 2019) 4. Axel Dreher, Adreas Fuchs et al, Banking on Beijing: The Aims and Impacts of China’s Overseas Development Program (Cambridge, 2022) 5. Austin Strange, Chinese Global Infrastructure (Cambridge Elements, 2024), https://www.cambridge.org/core/elements/chinese-global- infrastructure/35932BF8AEADDEFF1E96B19B13300FAE (free download) C) Writing Requirements 1. One short (500-750 words) critical response paper: due by the end of Tuesday 17 September(10 %) 2. One short (1,000- 1,250 word ) policy brief : due end of Week Eight before class on Friday 24 October (15%) 3. One abstract/ short bibliography for final essay/ policy report : not formally assessed but necessary to finalize your topics. DUE BEFORE the end of MONDAY 11 November . This will not be graded, but is important for feedback prior to your presentations. 4. One policy report OR regular analytical academic essay on a topic involving China and the Global South that covers some aspect of China’s investment/ aid/projects/ trade/ migration / environmental impact etc. You do not have to choose a topic that is explicitly covered in this class, but it should broadly align with the themes of the course and not be primarily focused on either military or security issues. (5,000-7,000 words), due BEFORE the beginning of regular exams on Monday 15 December 2024 (50%) D) Oral Requirements 1. One 20 minute oral + ppt presentation on your chosen topic for your final policy report/ paper, date TBA in either Week 11 or Week 12 (15%) 2. Regular participation and preparation in seminar discussions. (10%) This breaks down into two components: a. Taking on presentation of the seminar readings for the week and participating in other exercises b. Regular attendance in class (attendance will be taken from Week Three, and without a reasonable excuse, deductions will be made for non-attendance) c. Regular and meaningful participation and discussion even when you are not a presenter Statement on Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in this class Artificial Intelligence is an increasingly powerful, and also easily misused, tool that researchers and writers at any level now cannot afford to ignore. I encourage the critical use of AI in this class (it is very helpful for organizing thoughts, sifting through references and bibliography, and checking text. However, the uncritical and unrestricted use of AI can equally lead to very large problems (false or misleading information, “tilt” towards what is popular rather than what is well referenced and well argued, overreliance on what is current and trendy rather than what has depth and might be older). Think of AI as an autocompletion and sorting tool: it can help you sort and get through routine tasks quickly, but it cannot substitute for either your thinking or the parameters that you put in when you ask it to do something. Therefore, the critical use of AI in this class is not only permitted, but encouraged. However, I do require that you indicate exactly when and how you use AI in all your written work. Schedule of Class Sessions: PART I: The Background [History matters] Week One [Friday 5 September]: Introductions, explanations, and reading texts on China and the Global South Readings, charts, and background on China’s domestic politics and policy making: https://multimedia.scmp.com/widgets/china/cpc- primer/?fbclid=IwAR0wOmmNM8myoMAf4qSgslc08d3eKk6THMEnvBb- WcauiKt8kVpobAsul2c Meg Rithmire, “Going Out or Opting Out? Capital, Political Vulnerability, and the State in China’s Outward Investment”, Harvard Business School Working Paper 20-009, https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/20-009_664c9264-f0ee- 4e43-acbd-d5da9f08caf1.pdf David Lampton, Selina Ho, and Cheng-chwee Kuik, Rivers of Iron: Railroads and Chinese Power in Southeast Asia University of California Press, 2020, pp. ix-xv For reference: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Chinese-Communist-Party-Government- Structure_fig2_228409863?fbclid=IwAR1XZJODNq4lhAbYXcrZLfA5Sb2IICVe5E 7n2_KlmgnfxP707Fo2rukr-2A https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/chinese-communist- party?fbclid=IwAR3WMfeeXbFIUwVXsFWh1VOcTGqxE0gsDG9anaKOQhmXw uBdhb2tyIYrFrU Kenneth Lieberthal, Governing China: From Revolution Through Reform 2nd edition, Norton, pp. 3-26, 171-240. (introduction, and parts of chapters 6 and 7). The Lieberthal reading is old, but is still one of the better explanations of a political system that is often opaque. Recommended: Julia C. Strauss, “The Past in the Present: Historical and Rhetorical Lineages in China’s Relations with Africa”, The China Quarterly 199, September 2009, pp. 777– 795, doi:10.1017/S0305741009990208 PART I – The Grand Principles and Core Institutions Behind China’s Engagement with the Global South Week Two [Friday, 12 September] Ideals and Institutions: What is the Belt and Road Initiative [BRI], and how is it implemented? {aka “Follow the Money”} Readings: “Full text of President Xi's speech at opening of Belt and Road forum,” Xinhua, May 14, 2017 http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2017-05/14/c_136282982.htm Min Ye, The Belt Road and Beyond: State-Mobilized Globalization in China: 1998–2018 (Cambridge University Press, 2020), pp. 26-49 Yuen Yuen Ang. “Demystifying China’s Belt and Road: The Struggle to Define China’s Project of the Century,” Foreign Affairs, May 22, 2019 https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/china/2019-05-22/demystifying-belt-and- road Brahma Chellaney. “China’s debt trap diplomacy.” Project Syndicate. Jan 23, 2017. https://www.project-syndicate.org/commentary/china-one-belt-one-road-loans- debt-by-brahma-chellaney-2017-01 John Hurley, Scott Morris, and Gailyn Portelance. “Examining the debt implications of the BRI from a policy perspective.” Center for Global Development. Lina Benabdallah, “Contesting the international order by integrating it: the case of China’s Belt and Road Initiative”, Third World Quarterly 40:1, pp. 92-108, DOI: 10.1080/01436597.2018.1529539 ASSIGNMENT 1: CRITICAL RESPONSE PAPER Due by the END OF TUESDAY 16 SEPTEMBER Moramudali and Panduwawala offer one version of China’s lending and “debt diplomacy” in Sri Lanka and Sarvananthan suggests quite another. Write a critical response paper of around 750 words in which you engage the following question: Is China engaged in “debt diplomacy” in Sri Lanka? In addition to the Moramundi/ Panduwawala and Sarvananthan, Chellaney, Himmer/Rod, and Brautigam are worth consulting. The Primary readings to consult for this exercise are below: Umesh Moramudali and Thilina Panduwawala “Evolution of Chinese Lending to Sri Lanka Since the mid-2000s – Separating Myth from Reality”, CARI Policy Brief No 22 November 2022 Available at SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4305736 And Muttukrishna Sarvananthan, “Chinese Lending to Sri Lanka: a Factual Cum 'Reality' Check: a Rejoinder to Umesh Moramudali and Thilina Panduwawala (February 26, 2023). Available at SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4369990 or http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4369990. This said, you’ll have to refer to the Chellany article, which is foundational, and it might be useful to consult Hurley et al, and Brautigam from next week. docs.text: 1 Updated June 7, 2024 Fall Semester 2024 Government and Politics in Asia (a two-credit course) Instructor: Tun-jen Cheng (tjchen@wm.edu or tjcheng7@gmail.com) Class hours: 9-11 am Tuesday Taiwan time, Fall 2024 Office hours: 3-5pm Wednesday, Taiwan time, for the first 7 weeks; thereafter 7-9 pm Wednesday Taiwan time; by appointment, please email two preferred time slots to Allan and me two days in advance to schedule a half-an-hour meeting Description: In half a century Asia has emerged as the most vibrant economic region on earth. It is essential to understand political underpinnings and consequences of this region’s economic transformation. Covering East Asia, Southeast Asia, and South Asia, this course is structured thematically. Within each theme, however, we will focus on country specific cases that are either standing alone or in paired or multiple comparisons, thereby combining thematic analysis and country specificities. Part I provides a historical and contemporary overview of Asian politics, examining dynasty legacy, colonial rule, decolonization, and state- and nation-building. For Part II, this seminar addresses salient aspects of regime dynamics in the context of economic development which is the most important goal for a country upon gaining political independence. Topic issues for these five sessions include regime type and economic growth, drivers, processes, and problems of democratic transitions, as well as patterns of political evolution. For Part III, this seminar dwells on political institutions and processes in Asian democracies, covering constitutional forms of government, political parties, political participation, political polarization, and contentious politics. The final part is devoted to a few leading issues of governance in resilient authoritarian politics, including the implicit social contract, the political and economic conundrum, and intractable agency problems. Please note that the class and office hours will be in person during the first seven sessions; thereafter you continually come to our classroom while the instructor conducts the sessions remotely on GoogleMeet. Course requirements and grade distribution: 20% Attendance and participation 30% Midterm assignment (due 5pm Oct 21, 2024 Monday, Week VIII) 50% Term paper (due 5pm December 30, 2024 Monday, Week XVII) Reading materials for the course: All required readings are book chapters or journal articles. They will be available to you in softcopy. Note that a few book chapters are from the following three Routledge Handbooks: Tun-jen Cheng and Yun-han Chu, eds., Routledge Handbook of Democratization in East Asia, 2018; Paul Brass, ed. Routledge Handbook of South Asia Politics, 2012; Jeffrey Haynes, ed., Routledge Handbook of Democratization, 2010 [in which Southeast cases are predominant examples]. You are encouraged to but have no obligation to read any recommended readings. In addition, the instructor will inform you before each session which items in the required readings are for you to dive in, which other items are for you to skim over only. 2 Weekly Topics Part I. Pre-colonial Legacy, De-colonization, State-Building, and Nation-Building Sessions 1 & 2. Sept 3 & Sept 10 Course mechanics and an overview of Asian politics: patterns, distinct features, and puzzles;Pre-colonial and colonial legacies, decolonization, state-building and nation-building Required readings: Nayan Chanta, “When Asia was one,” Global Asia 2003, pp.58- 68; Chun-in Moon and Seung-won Suh, “Burden of the Past: history, identity, and nationalism in Northeast Asia,” Global Asia 2004, pp.34-48; Yuhua Wang, The Rise and Fall of Imperial China, Princeton University Press 2022, ch.1, pp.3-29. Recommended reading: Selections from Ebrey, Walthall, and Palais, East Asia, Houghton Mifflin 2009, pp.257-261, 296-303; Ian Talbot, “India and Pakistan: Colonialism, Nationalism, and Independence”; in Paul Brass ed., Routledge Handbook of South Asian Politics 2010, pp.27-41. Session 3. Sept 17 Mid-autumn holiday; no class; morning hours individual consultation hours (optional; by appointment) Part II Regime Dynamics and Economic Development Session 4. Sept 24 State capacity and economic development Required readings: Atul Kohli, State-Directed Development, Cambridge University Press, 2004, Ch 1 Introduction pp.1-26; Ch 2 The Colonial Origins of a Modern Political Economy: The Japanese Lineage of Korea’s Cohesive-Capitalist State, pp. 27-61, and Ch 6 “Origins of a Fragmented-Multiclass State and a Sluggish Economy: Colonial India,” pp.221-256. Recommended readings: Nicola Mastrorocco and Edoardo Teso, State Capacity as an Organizational Problem: the US experience, NBER August 21, 2023; Guo Xu, “The Cost of Patronage: Evidence from the British Empire,” American Economic Review 2018. Session 5. Oct 1 Regime type and economic change Required readings: Devin Joshi, “Multiparty Democracy and Economic Growth,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy, 2014, pp.25-46; John Harriss, “Political Change, Political Structure, and Indian State Since Independence,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp.55-66; Stuart Corbridge, “The Political Economy of Development in India Since Independence,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp305-320; Shahid Javed Burki, “Pakistan’s Politics and its Economy,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp,83- 97; Stephen Haggard and Andrew MacIntyre, “The Political Economy of the Asian Economic Crisis,” Review of International Political Economy 5:3 (Autumn 1998), 381-392 Individual consultation hours on October 7 & 9 (by appointment) Session 6. Oct 8 Drivers and processes of democratic transition Required readings: Larry Diamond, The Spirit of Democracy, New York: Times Book 2009, ch 4 on the internal factors, pp.88-105, ch 5 on the external factors, pp.106-134, ch 6 on regional influence, pp.135-152, and ch 7 on what sustains democracy, pp.153- 3 168; Matthew Carlson, “East and Southeast Asia,” in Jeffrey Haynes, Routledge Handbook of Democratization, pp.129-144; Farida Jalazai, “Democracy in India and Pakistan: parallel past, divergent futures,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, pp.112- 128 Individual consultation hours on October 14 & 16 (by appointment) Session 7. Oct 15 Problems and challenges of new democracies Required readings: Thomas Carothers and Benjamin Press, “Understanding and Responding to Global Democratic Backsliding,” CEIP paper, 2022, pp.1-26; Tun-jen Cheng and Yun-han Chu, “An Overview of East Asian Democratization” and Yu- tzung Chang and Yun-han Chu, “East Asian Democratization in Comparative Perspective” both chapters in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook of Democratization in East Asia, 2018, pp.1-17 and pp.19-39; Thomas Bruneau, “The Military,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, pp.207-221; Stephen Cohen, “The Militaries of South Asia,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp,351-363 Midterm assignment due 5pm, October 21, Monday Session 8. Oct 22 Assessing India’s democracy under Modi: an in-depth case study Required readings: Sumit Ganguly, “Modi’s Undeclared Emergency,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.144-152; Maya Tudor, “Why India’s Democracy is Dying,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.121-132; Rahul Verma, “The Exaggerated Death of Indian Democracy,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.153- 161; Laura Gamboa, “How Oppositions Fight Back,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.90-104. Part III Democratic Institutions and Processes in Asia Session 9. Oct 29 Liberal democracy, electoral democracy and hybrid regime Required readings: Jorgen Moller, “The Gap between Electoral and Liberal Democracy Revisited,” Acta Politica, 42, 2007, pp.380-400; Gary Rodan and Kanishka Jayasuriya, “Hybrid Regimes,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook of Democratization, pp.175-189; William Case, “Politics in Malaysia Today—Demise of the Hybrid? Not So Fast,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy December 2019, pp.1-30 and his “Regime Type and Pandemic Policy: Hybrid Exceptionalism in Malaysia,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy December 2020, pp.31-56. Session 10. Nov 5 Constitutional form of government Required readings: Juan Linz, “The Perils of Presidentialism” Journal of Democracy 1990, pp.51-69; Marco Bunte and Mark R. Thompson, “Perlous Presidentialism in Southeast Asia,” in Contemporary Politics, 2018, 42:3; pp.251-265; Jiunn-rong Yeh, “Constitutionalism and Judicial Review in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.225-248; Tun-jen Cheng, “Political Institutions and the Malaise of East Asian New Democracies,” Journal of East Asian Studies, 2003:3; pp.1-41. Session 11. Nov 12 Political parties and party system Required readings: Vicky Randall, “Political Parties,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, 2007, pp.222-236; Allen Hicken and Erik Martinez Kuhonta, “Introduction: Rethinking Party System Institutionalization in Asia,” in their eds., 4 Party System Institutionalization in Asia, Cambridge University Press 2015, pp.1-24 Session 12. Nov 19 Political participation Required readings: Zhengxu Wang and Leihua Ye, “Political Participation in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.251-268; Min-hua Huang, “Cognitive Involvement and Democratic Understanding,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook 2018, pp.297-313; Pippa Norris, “Electoral Integrity in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp. 405-424 Session 13. Nov 26 Political polarization Required readings: Krige Siebrits, Economc Inequality and Political Polarization,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy, July 2022, pp.41-60; Gordon Crawford and Abdul- Gafaru Abdulai, “Democratization, Poverty and Inequality,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, pp.353-367; Nae Young Lee and Sung Min Han, “Politics of Party Polarization in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.193-208; Thomas Carothers and Andrew O’Donohue, eds., Political Polarization in South and Southeast Asia: Old Divisions and New Dangers, CEIP 2020, pp.1-109 (read its brief introduction and one country chapter that interests you most). Session 14. Dec 3 Contentious politics Required readings: Meredith Weiss, “Resistance and Resilience: Copying With/Against the State,” Journal of Social Science Issues in Southeast Asia, 32:2; 2017; pp.374-404; Sumanta Banerjee, “Radical and Violent Political Movements,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp.382-398; Stanley A Kochanek, “Corruption and the Criminalization of Politics in South Asia,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp.364- 381; review Laura Gamboa, “How Oppositions Fight Back,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.90-104 Part IV Governance in Asian Authoritarian Regimes Session 15. Dec 10 An overview of resilient authoritarian systems in Asia; the grand bargain and the political and economic conundrum in China Required readings: Andrew Nathan, “Resilient Authoritarianism,” Bruce Gilley, “The Limits of Resilient Authoritarianism,” both in Journal of Democracy, 2003, pp.6-17, 18-27; Jessica Teets, Civil Society under Authoritarianism: the China Model, Cambridge University Press, 2014, ch.1, pp.38-78; Wei Shan and Yongnien Zheng, “Geopolitics and Democratization in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.509-527; Jeremy Wallace, Cities and Stability, Oxford University Press, 2014, ch.3, pp.43-70 ; skim through Dali Yang, “China’s Developmental Authoritarianism: Dynamics and Pitfalls,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.122-141. Session 16. Dec 17 Intractable agency problems in China Required readings: Deborah Brown and Tun-jen Cheng, “The Vatican and the Chinese Party State: Where Do the Parallels End?” Orbis; Winter 2016, pp.72-86 Andrew Wedeman, “The Evolution of China’s Anti-Corruption Strategy,” in Cheng Chen and Meredith Weiss, eds., The Political Logics of Anticorruption Efforts in Asia, Albany: SUNY Press 2019, pp.201-228; Adam Posen, “The End of China’s Economic Miracle,” Foreign Affairs, August 2023, pp.1-8. 5 Midterm assignment: Pick a topic on political development or an essential aspect of political dimension of economic development in as many Asian nations as possible. Or you can pick two comparable cases. You can even do just one country. But no matter how many country cases you have, make good use of a database available in the field, and write a well-focused piece that is both theory informed and empirically substantiated. Term paper: You can pick a new topic or delve more in-depth into the topic that you have already dwelled on in your midterm paper. Consultation and mechanics of two writing projects: You are encouraged to come to my office for consultation for your topical choice. On both written assignments, you must provide appropriate citation for all thoughts, words, or ideas that are not your own (this includes the ideas of peers). An electronic file summarizing the Chicago Manual citation style will be posted on our class’ eeclass platform. The midterm assignment should be approximately 1500 words in length and the term paper approximately 3,000 words in length. Both should be submitted via email attachment in both Word and PDF formats. Both are to be turned in on time by 5 pm on the due date. Late submission triggers a loss of half a letter grade per day (that is, for an assignment turned in one day late and is an A quality one, the conferred grade will be A/A-; if it is turned in two days late, the conferred grade will be A-). AI policy: Using generative AI for this class is discouraged but not prohibited. Disclosure of its use is required. Expectations: • Class participation is a required part of the course. Please attend all classes and contribute towards discussion. • Writing, writing, writing: Learning to write well, to make a coherent and well researched argument, is one of the key skills you should get out of the grad school. • Current Events: A good theory, thesis, or analytical framework is a tool for digesting current events. Current events in turn allow us to assess the utility and limitation of the analytical tool. This is a very exciting time in Asian Politics with many daily changes in the region. I therefore strongly recommend that you follow current events in Asia by reading a major news source with good international coverage (i.e. BBC news, New York Times, The Economist etc.) or a news source from a subregion (i.e. Indian Express, Dawn, ToloNews etc.). This will help you get more out of the reading, by making class discussions more productive and improving the quality of your analytical thinking. docs.text: 1 Asian Development in Global Historical Perspective 歷史與全球觀點下的亞洲發展 Fall 2025 Instructor: R. Bin Wong, Distinguished Research Professor of History, UCLA Course Code TSE 602800 Place: Time: 10:10 AM – 1:00 PM Course Overview This course focuses on Asian economic development within a global context of industrialization & trade beginning in the late eighteenth century, moving through the 19th & 20th centuries, and looking forward into future 21st-c. possibilities. Central to this course are the economic and political principles and practices that together form the political economies of the past, present, and our possible futures. Each of the course’s four units devotes time to relationships between economic development and the natural environment in order to place our contemporary concerns about climate change in historical perspective and prepare future paths of economic and environmental change. Late 20th-century scientific research began to accumulate evidence confirming multiple ways in which the benefits of economic growth came at serious costs to the health of the natural environment and its plant and animal life. We therefore consider how the processes of modern industrialization that began less than 250 years ago depend on natural resources in ways unimaginable for most of the 300,000 years of human history. We begin in Unit I looking at Asian Development in the 19th-20th c. world of economic change and move in Unit II to placing Asian development within a global economic and environmental framework. The first half of the course brings us to the late 20th century and the recognition of limits to growth that leads us to Unit III where 21st-century efforts to foster sustainable development confront the challenges of achieving sustainability transformations. Unit IV concludes the course’s concern for understanding how economic activity depends on natural resources with a focus on energy development that is foundational to the economic security and wellbeing of people across Asia and the rest of the world. 2 Each of the four units considers relationships between economic development and the natural environment in order to place our contemporary concerns about climate change in historical perspective. Central to this course are the economic and political principles and practices that together form the political economies of the past, present, and possible futures we seek to create. This course aims to make your study of political economy prepare you to consider the type of 21st-century political economy you want to see emerge. Course Format 1. We meet in Weeks 1-5 and Weeks 7-12. Each three-hour session will include both lecture and discussion components. Weekly Study Guides with questions that highlight key themes to think about as you prepare the upcoming meeting’s readings will be posted to the class website at least a week in advance of the class meeting. Students are encouraged to take notes that summarize your understanding of the articles or portions of books that makes up each week’s readings. Having these notes will help you participate actively in each class as well as help you prepare the written work assigned in this course. Please be aware that you have readings to prepare before our first class meeting. 2. Readings for each class meeting can be found on our class website course syllabus links. 3. Please consider sending me an email by Tuesday evening regarding any questions you may have about any of week’s readings that I will try to address in my opening remarks. The more communication we have, the more effectively the course will succeed in teaching you ways to understand economic development. 4. Students will write and submit digitally three Response Essays that address one or more of the questions raised on the weekly study guides. The first Response Essay (1000 – 1500 words) will cover Units I & II and be due on October 9th (Week 6) at 1:00 pm. The second and third Response Essays (750-1250 words each) will cover Units III and IV respectively and be due on Saturdays (1:00 pm ) of Weeks 9 and 12. 5. These Response Essays along with the Study Guide notes you take on the weekly readings should prepare you for class lecture and discussion; they should also provide much of the basis for you to write your Final Papers. 6. Citations Format for the Response Essays and Final Paper should be made in a social science format of brief in-text citations (Author or Lead Author followed by “et al.”, then 3 publication date followed by page number(s)” and a bibliography organized by author or lead author’s last name followed by publication date and the title of book, book chapter or article; if you cite any PPT lecture material, in-text citation should be PPT title and slide number(s) and in the bibliography as “my name, week number, and PPT Title.” 7. The Final Paper assignment will be a 1,750-2,500-word double-spaced (7-10 pp) essay response to some selection of course themes. While I will offer you some themes for your final papers during Unit III, you can either select among the themes I suggest or propose your own theme. You’re encouraged to do some additional reading for your final paper. In past years, some students have incorporated materials regarding their home countries as part of the preparation of their final papers. Finally, I ask that you inform me by email the topic you choose for your final paper no later than Wednesday November 12th. Final papers are due Week 14 on Thursday December 11th by 5:00 pm TST. 8. Grading Please inform me if for any reason you will not be attending class as this is the norm typical in graduate school training (which a few students in the past did not realize). While there is no grading of class participation, there is an expectation of oral engagement with course material during class each week and if you’re not able to attend a class session, you’ll be expected to write some brief responses to the Study Guide Questions. Each Response Essay counts as 20% of your final course grade and the final paper 40% of your final course grade. The papers will have numerical grades converted to a final letter grade according to: A+ (97–100), A (93–96), A- (90–92), B+ (87–89), B (83–86), B- (80–82), C+ (77–79), C (73–76), C- (70–72), D+ (67–69), D (65–66), D- (below 65). To summarize, each paper gets a numerical grade with the sum of the numerical grades adding up to a potential maximum of 100 points. Ethics Statement on Generative Artificial Intelligence Grounded in the principles of transparency and responsibility, this course encourages students to leverage AI for developing their understanding of course materials. In accordance with the published Guidelines for Collaboration, Co-learning, and 4 Cultivation of Artificial Intelligence Competencies in University Education, this course adopts the following policy: Conditionally Open If you use generative AI in any of the four writing assignments, you must briefly explain how you used generative AI to develop your understanding of specific concepts, themes, arguments, and research methodologies in the readings. This explanation should be given below your paper title. If usage is discovered without proper disclosure, instructors, the institution, or relevant units have the right to reevaluate the assignment or report or withhold scores. I have not used generative AI to develop course materials or format. List of Unit Subjects, Session Themes, and the Readings I. Asian Development in the 19th-20th c. World of Economic Change A. Origins, spread, and limits of Industrialization (Week 1 September 4) Readings: Allen 2011, “Why the industrial revolution was British.” Allen 2014, “The spread of manufacturing.” Jun, Lewis, Kang, 2008 “Korean Expansion and Decline from the Seventeenth to the Nineteenth Century: A View Suggested by Adam Smith.” Elson, 1993 “International Commerce, the State and Society: Economic and Social Change.” B. Capitalism: Fossil fuels, the Environment & the Geopolitical World Order (Week 2 September 11) Readings: Wrigley, 2013 “Energy and the English Industrial Revolution.” Tello-Aragay & Jover-Avellà, 2014 “Economic History & the Environment” Sugihara, 2017 “Monsoon Asia, Intra-regional trade and fossil fuel-driven industrialization.” Wong, 2021 “Modern Capitalism’s Multiple Pasts and Its Possible Future” II. 20th c. Asian Development in a Global Economic & Environmental Frames A. Asian Economic Growth (Week 3 September 18) 5 Readings: Fukao and Settsu, 2021 “Japan-Modern Economic Growth in Asia.” Grove and Kubo, 2022 “Handicraft and Modern Industries.” (China) Wu and Fan 2014 “China’s Economic Reform: Processes, issues, and prospects (1978-2012)” in Chow and Perkins eds., Routledge Handbook of the Chinese Economy Huff, 2021 “Growth and Globalization Phases in South East Asian Development.” B. 20th century Energy and Environment (Week 4 September 25) Readings: Bankoff, 1995 “Coming to terms with nature--state & environment in maritime Southeast Asia” McNeill, 2007 “Social, Economic, and Political Forces in Environmental Change” Mattick, Williams & Allenby, 2010 “Historical Trends in Global Energy Consumption” Meadows et al 1972 The Limits to Growth chapter 1 C. 20th-century Knowledge & Beliefs About Development (Week 5 October 2) Readings: Meadows et al 1972 The Limits to Growth Chs 2 & 3; Meadows, 2007 “Evaluating Past Forecasts--reflections on one critique of Limits to Growth” Week 6 No class 1st Paper Assignment due October 9 at 1:00 pm III. Late 20th-c. Recognition of Limits to Growth & Early 21st-c. Efforts to Foster Sustainable Development A. Limits to Growth & the Pursuit of Sustainable Development (Week 7 October 16) Readings: Meadows et al 1972 Chs 4 & 5; Gale 2018 Ch 1 & Ch 3 B. 21st c. views of sustainable development (Week 8 October 23) Readings: 2004 Meadows, Dixson-Declève et al Earth for All Chs 1, 8; 2018 Gale Ch 4 Creating sustainability value & sustainability transformation C. Sustainability Value and Leverage Points for Sustainability Transformation (Week 9 October 30) 6 Readings: 2018 Gale Ch 8; 2017 Abson Leverage Points; 2019 Fischer & Riechers Leverage Points Perspective; 2021 Linnér and Wibeck Drivers of sustainability transformations--leverage points, contexts, & conjunctures IV. Asian Energy & Sustainable Development in Geopolitics & the Global Economy A. SDGs: Asia in Global Perspective & Systems Thinking (Week 10 November 6) Readings: 2018 Gale Ch 5 pp 123-127; 2025 ESCAP Asia & the Pacific SDG Progress Report (6-7, 26-31)—2020 Fortier Connecting the SDG Dots Through Systems Thinking (7 pp), 2014 Weitz et al A Nexus Approach—Formulating Integrated Water, Energy, and Food SDGs (15 pp) B. Asian energy development, especially in & by China (Week 11 November 13) Readings: 2024 IEA China’s evolving footprint (10 pp); 2025 Nedopil China BRI 2024 investment report; 2023 Liu et al China BRI energy (24 pp) ; 2025 Chiengkul Toward greener BRI (22 pp) C. Energy Transitions & Connectivity in Asia (Week 12 November 20) Readings: 2024 ESCAP Energy connectivity for sustainable development in Asia & the Pacific (pp 1-41 [Executive Summary, Introduction, Ch 1, Ch 2]; 54-69 [Ch 4]); 2024 IEA SE Asia Energy Outlook Report (pp 5-45; 124-192)

docs.text: 1 Political Economy of the Semiconductor Industry Course Outline The semiconductor industry has become strategically important in economic growth and international relations. This course is designed to demystify the complexity of the global semiconductor industry in terms of technological development, market competition, geopolitics, and interactions of national policies. It is an interdisciplinary course bringing together the knowledge of engineering, management, economics, and political science. The course is divided into four parts and to be taught by four instructors, with each instructor covering a part of the course. The rest of the time will be used for examination and guest lectures. The four parts are (1) development of the semiconductor industry and technology, (2) characteristics and evolutions of the global semiconductor market, (3) geo-politics and geo-economics in the semiconductor industry, (4) technology policies pertinent to the semiconductor industry in East Asia. The detailed contents of each part are listed below. Topic II: How Taiwan developed its semiconductor industry (1975-1994). Topic III: Important technological breakthroughs in the semiconductor industry. Reference: • John Matthews 1995, “High-tech Industrialization in East Asia: the case of the semiconductor industry in Taiwan and Korea” CIER • 張如心， 「矽說台灣」 ， 潘文淵文教基金會， 天下文化出版， 2006 • 史欽泰、陳添枝、吳淑敏「從邊緣到核心:台灣半導體如何成為台灣的 • 心臟」，天下文化出版， 2025 • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_transistor • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microprocessor • Shih, W., Shih, C., and Chien, Chen-Fu (2008), Horizontal specialization and modularity in the semiconductor industry, Harvard Business School Case Study (9-609-001). • Shih, W., Chien, Chen-Fu, Shih, C., and Chang, J. (2009), The TSMC Way: Meeting Customer Needs at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., Harvard Business School Case Study (9-610-003). Part 2 Global Semiconductor Market Description: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the global semiconductor market and supply chains. Students will gain an in-depth understanding of the political and economic factors that drive the semiconductor industry, including market trends, supply chain dynamics, and the role of Taiwan in the industry. The course will cover key topics such as the semiconductor market by industry, by technology, and by region; the semiconductor supply chains; and 3 future challenges and opportunities in the semiconductor industry. Through lectures, case studies, discussions, and projects, students will develop a strong foundation in the political economy of the semiconductor industry and its role in global economics. Learning Outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: • Understand the political and economic factors driving the global semiconductor market • Analyze trends in the semiconductor industry by industry, technology, and region • Understand the dynamics of the semiconductor supply chain • Assess the role of Taiwan in the semiconductor industry • Identify future challenges and opportunities in the semiconductor industry Course Topics: • Overview of the Global Semiconductor Industry • Market Trends by Industry, Technology, and Region • The Semiconductor Supply Chains • The Role of Taiwan in the Semiconductor Industry • Future Challenges and Opportunities in the Semiconductor Industry Recommended Reading: • Chris Miller, 2022, Chip War: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology, London: Simon and Schuster. • Stephen Witt, 2025, The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip, Viking Book. Part 3 Geo-politics and Geo-economics Topic I: Foundry Model: The origin of the foundry model; why Taiwan came to adopt the foundry model; the impacts of the foundry model and TSMC’s success. Topic II: US-Japan trade conflicts: Trade war on semiconductors; SEMATECH (US industrial policy to revitalize the semiconductor industry); the impacts of geopolitics on the semiconductor Topic III: China’s rise: China’s rise in the semiconductor industry; industrial policy; role of the state; US-China technology war and threats on globalization. Topic IV: DRAM: Role of DRAM in the semiconductor industry; US-Japan competition; Japan-Korea competition; China’s challenge. Topic V: Moore’s Law: Effects of Moore’s Law; Barriers to Moore’s Law and technology progress; Scale economies and industry structures. 4 Recommended Readings: Craig Addison, 2001, Silicon Shield: Taiwan’s Protection against Chinese Attack, Nashville, TN: The Fusion Press. docs.text: 1 COURSE SYLLABUS COURSE TITLE: International organizations in global politics Autumn 2025 • Credit: 2 • Time: T7T8 (Tuesday 15:30~16:20, 16:30~17:20) • Room: A10, TSE • Level: MA and PhD • Instructor : Gerald Chan, e-mail: cgcw@mx.nthu.edu.tw; gerald.chan@auckland.ac.nz • Office: C03, TSE • Office hour: Wednesday 13:00~15:00 or by appointment • Teaching assistant: TBC COURSE DESCRIPTION This course assesses the significance of international organizations in global politics. It focuses on the theoretical approaches to the study of international organizations, including the origins and development of these global bodies, especially the growth of regional organizations after the Second World War. The course explores the changing roles, functions and norms of these organizations working in such areas as security, economics, environment protection, human rights, public health, resource scarcity, science and technology, and social justice. How does the rise of Asian countries, in particular China, affect inter-state relations and the workings of international organizations? KEYWORDS International organizations, global issues, political economy, norms and rules, Asia, China LECTURE DATES & TOPICS Sep 2 Introduction Sep 9 Lecture 1 (L1): Globalization Sep 16 L2: Global governance Sep 23 L3: International organizations Sep 30 L4: Peace and security Oct 7 L5: Trade and finance Oct 14 L6: Environmental protection Oct 21 L7: Human rights Oct 28 L8: Humanitarian intervention Nov 4 L9: Public health 2 Nov 11 L10: Resource security Nov 18 L11: Poverty Nov 25 L12: Development Dec 2 L13: The digital world [Course instructor on conference leave] Dec 9 L14: Summary and conclusion Dec 16 Exam AIMS AND OBJECTIVES At the end of the course, we should be able to: 1. understand international relations and organisations in their many facets; 2. make a distinction between globalisation as a process and as an ideology; 3. examine the roles and functions of international organisations in conflict and cooperation; 4. assess the impact of the rise and fall of great powers on globalisation and global governance; and 5. probe a little into the future shape of globalisation. TEACHING METHOD Weekly lectures and/or tutorials/seminars where students make presentations for class discussion (to be arranged). ASSESSMENT Three pieces of assessment (details to be arranged): 1. 50% research essay a. Topic on some aspects of globalisation, global governance, or international organisation (to be discussed) b. Word limit: 3,000 words (plus or minus 10%) c. Essay due: 9 December 2024, 5pm (no extension please, except for unforeseen circumstances) 2. 40% written exam: TBA 3. 10% class presentation and discussion RULES ON THE USE OF AI We shall discuss this issue at our introductory meeting, so that we can have a common understanding between students and the teacher as to what to expect from each other. 3 A general rule: Conditionally open; please specify how generative AI will be used in course output. docs.text: TSE 604900: Institutions and Economic Development Course Description The purpose of this course is to analyze institutions, and how institutions affect economic development. In addition to general analyses, institutions of China and China’s development are discussed with some details. The institutional component introduces analytical concepts and theoretical frameworks with historical and contemporary contexts. The economic component addresses economic development and political economic issues. It is a largely self-contained course on institutional economics, political economics, and Chinese political economy. Basic microeconomics and macroeconomics, development economics, political science, Chinese political economy are beneficial, but not as prerequisite knowledge. Basic Text Chenggang Xu (2025), Lecture Notes (PPT) (to be distributed during lectures). You are welcome to challenge the arguments and evidence presented in the lectures and basic readings, but you must do so explicitly and support your position with well-reasoned counterarguments and properly sourced evidence. Otherwise, your answers will be considered a failure to understand the course materials. Rules on the use of AI and Online Information A substantial portion of this course is based on recent research findings published in 2025, many of which are not yet widely available on the internet or incorporated into AI chatbot training. Therefore, you should focus on the material presented in lectures, PowerPoint slides, basic text and main references of the course, rather than relying on internet sources or AI chatbots. You are fully responsible for any misleading or incorrect answers obtained from internet sources or chatbots. If you choose to use AI chatbots as an assistant in preparing group presentations, you must do the following: 1. Report the questions (prompts) you asked the chatbot. 2. Provide your judgment on whether the chatbot's response was correct/incorrect, and explain why. 3. Describe how you ultimately arrived at the outcome you believe is correct.

docs.text: 1 Trade and Regulations in the Digital Age Fall 2025 Professor Shin-yi PENG W6W7@TSE Overview This course examines international trade and regulations in the context of the digital economy. Newspaper headlines frequently highlight global trade challenges in the digital age, from disputes over semiconductor tariffs and national security-based 5G standards to data nationalism measures that restrict cross-border data flows. Governments are facing dilemmas between, on the one hand, maximizing opportunities stemming from the digital economy and, on the other, managing the associated risks and pursuing public policy objectives such as privacy and cybersecurity. The course begins by exploring regulatory frameworks for information and communication technology (ICT) products, with a particular focus on international trade rules and related disputes. It then turns to data-related domestic regulations, analyzing their impact on global trade and the balance among trade liberalization, industrial innovation, and digital sovereignty, particularly a nation’s right to regulate amid rising geopolitical tensions. Students will also study the role of international trade rules under the World Trade Organization (WTO), free trade agreements (FTAs), and digital economy agreements (DEAs) in shaping the digital economy. They will examine the interests of key stakeholders in international negotiations and identify areas where new trade rules and policies may be needed. Schedule (Provisional) Week 1 (9/3) Trade in Goods: Overview ICT Industrial Policy and Trade Rules Week 2 (9/10) Tariff War over Technology Export Controls on ICT Products Week 3 (9/17) Digital Economy and National Security Class Exercise: Moot Problem on ICT Trade Week 4 (9/24) International Standardization of ICT Products 2 Technical Barriers to Trade in ICT Products Week 5 (10/1) Trade in Services: Overview Digital Sovereignty and the Right to Regulate Week 6 (10/8) WTO Jurisprudence and Digital Trade Digital Services: Classification and Market Access Week 7 (10/15) Privacy, Cybersecurity and Global Trade Governance Week 8 (10/22) General and Security Exceptions to Digital Trade Rules Week 9 (10/29) No Class due to the University’s Annual Sports Day Week 10 (11/5) Data Nationalism and Data Localization Class Exercise: Multistakeholder Role-Playing Meeting on Data Localization Issues Week 11 (11/12) Digital Trade Rules in FTAs and DEAs Week 12 (11/19) Digital Platform and Trade Governance Week 13 (11/26) Artificial Intelligence and International Trade Law Week 14 (12/3) Digital Inclusion, Investment and Sustainability Class Exercise: Trade Negotiations Simulation Week 15 (12/10) Student Presentations Week 16 (12/17) Student Presentations Assessment Class participation (50%) Research paper (50%) A more detailed e-version of the syllabus, with reading materials and class exercises, will be provided in class.
